bsk1-sociology: Both develop sociological theories of institutions, inequality and social change relevant to governing society.
bsk1-economics: Both introduce microeconomic and macroeconomic reasoning about markets, incentives and public choices.
bsk1-policy: Both examine policy-making phases, competing interpretations and public decisions. UCR uses a sugar-policy case across national and international arenas, rather than the same introductory policy-science syllabus.
bsk1-politics: Both examine political institutions, democracy and different national political systems; UCR adds comparative empirical inquiry.
bsk1-law: Both examine public authority through legal principles and institutions; UCR also surveys private law and social justice.
bsk1-statistics: Both teach descriptive statistics, association, estimation and hypothesis testing for empirical research; UCR also integrates research design and a group project.
bsk1-organisations: Both examine organisational structures, culture, leadership and behaviour; UCR approaches these through organisational psychology rather than exclusively public organisations.
bsk1-management: Negotiating with stakeholders and handling power, conflict and relationships addresses an identifiable part of public managers’ outward and internal work. UCR does not reproduce the full public-management, financial or crisis-management curriculum.
bsk2-public-econ: Both examine public goods, market failure, taxation, spending and government intervention.
bsk2-quant: Both develop regression-based inference for social questions. UCR extends into econometric estimators and tests, rather than reproducing every public-administration application.
bsk2-eu: Both examine EU institutions, actors, legitimacy and policy processes.
bsk2-international: International organisations and the legal rules governing cross-border collective action are a substantive common object. UCR emphasises international legal principles, rather than the full organisational study of international administration.
bsk2-digital: AI fairness, privacy, responsibility and political risk address an important part of governing digital technology. UCR is an AI ethics course; Leiden additionally studies public digital services, social media, data science and other government technology domains.
bsk2-affairs: Both examine strategic persuasion, framing and public-facing communication. UCR applies these in community and municipal sustainability projects, rather than a dedicated lobbying and interest-representation course.
bsk2-implementation: Both examine policy effectiveness, stakeholder interests and evaluation. UCR develops governance diagnosis and policy advice for sustainability issues, without reproducing the entire implementation/evaluation sequence.
bsk2-finance: Both examine budgeting, costing, organisational control and investment decisions. UCR teaches accounting and corporate finance rather than the public budget cycle, intergovernmental finance and Dutch public-sector rules.
bsk2-philosophy: Both examine political authority, rights and competing normative visions of governing. UCR surveys political thought rather than a public-administration-specific treatment.
bsk2-project: Both develop evidence-based policy reports about contested public problems. UCR uses conflict analysis, a policy brief and research dossier rather than Leiden’s group qualitative investigation of multi-level governance.
bsk3-ethics: Both develop and apply ethical theories to questions of action and responsibility. UCR addresses general ethical problems rather than specialising in public officials and administrative institutions.
bsk3-leadership: Both examine leadership, ethical judgment and communication. UCR uses leader interviews and an advisory report, rather than focusing exclusively on public leadership.
bsk3-law: Both study constitutional powers and administrative constraints, including participation, remedies and procedural fairness. UCR is comparative rather than a dedicated Dutch constitutional and administrative law course.
bsk2-qual: Both develop qualitative research design, interviews, coding, interpretation and reflexive inquiry; UCR is not restricted to public-administration applications.

blanks.bsk1-intro: Comparative politics and sustainability governance provide related institutional perspectives, but no selected course reproduces this integrated introduction to public administration as a discipline.
blanks.bsk1-history: General modern sociology and political thought do not establish Leiden’s specific Dutch political-administrative history from around1650 to the present.
blanks.bsk1-methods: Research design is substantively present within the UCR statistics and qualitative-methods courses, shown against their strongest respective counterparts. No separate selected course supplies this additional social-science foundations component.
blanks.bsk1-project: Municipal communication and other applied projects do not establish the specific empirical investigation of responsive government and tailored public service in this required integrative project.
blanks.bsk2-foundations: General ethics and political philosophy do not reproduce this component’s epistemology, scientific demarcation and foundations of public-administration knowledge.
blanks.bsk3-thesis: No scheduled course establishes a completed15ECindividual Public Administration thesis. Optional independent research is shown under the standard comparison rule outside scheduled180EC.
blanks.bsk3-electives: Genuine open elective space has no predetermined substantive counterpart.

audience.programmeDescription: Public Administration examines how governments and public organisations make decisions, manage institutions and respond to societal problems. This comparison follows Leiden’s Policy, Public Administration and Organisation route, with dedicated policy, management, law and research training.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR programmes approach public decisions through different combinations: policy and organisations; economics, accounting and management; or data, AI and public accountability. They offer substantive related study but do not reproduce Leiden’s continuous public-administration sequence, Dutch administrative history and law, integrative government projects or required individual thesis.

curriculum.limitation: The route totals 180 EC: 60 EC in each year, including 30 EC of open study and a 15-EC individual thesis. Thesis entry requires 115 eligible EC with specified methods and project requirements; minor, elective and internship credits cannot replace the required compulsory credits. First-year mentorship is mandatory without additional EC. Internships are optional and cannot coincide with the thesis.

componentNotes.bsk3-thesis: Required 15-EC individual empirical thesis. Entry requires a passed first year (60 EC), Quantitative Methods (5 EC), Qualitative Methods (5 EC), Integrative Project II (5 EC) and 40 EC of other compulsory later-year courses. Eligibility is checked on 1 August or 15 January; block-two resits do not count for spring entry. A thesis and internship cannot run concurrently.
componentNotes.bsk3-electives: 30 EC of open study, normally in the first semester of year three. Minor, exchange and elective approvals depend on the selection. Optional 15/30-EC internships require 90 earned programme EC including the first year, prior approval and 400/816 hours respectively.
componentNotes.bsk1-project: Required group research project with mandatory meetings, presentation and peer review. The exam and group paper must each pass.
componentNotes.bsk2-project: Required qualitative research project with assessed group work, participation and individual reflection. Methods and related governance courses are advised preparation.

concepts: A broad public-administration programme examining how governments and public organisations make, justify and implement decisions. Political science, law, sociology, economics, leadership and communication are combined with quantitative and qualitative research and applied policy analysis.

Focuses on how economic institutions, incentives, public finance, organisations and management shape government choices. Economics, accounting and econometrics are integrated with politics, law, sociology, strategy, leadership and qualitative research.

Examines how data, algorithms and artificial intelligence transform public decisions, organisations and citizen-state relations. Technical foundations in programming, data science and AI are combined with ethics, law, politics, sociology, leadership and governance research.
finding: All placements independently challenged. Correct statistical/political-philosophy/ethics matches, accounting/publicfinance and real policy-analysis correspondences replace generic weak matches.
